title: Feasibility study of two-stage direct laser acceleration of electrons
abstract: We present the first numerical demonstration of two-stage direct laser acceleration (DLA) of electrons. The result was obtained using quasi-3D particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations. The first stage ($a_0 = 6$, $τ= 200~\mathrm{fs}$, $w = 4λ$, $λ= 0.8~μ\mathrm{m}$) utilized a nitrogen gas target with an atomic density of $n_a = 0.008n_{cr}$. This stage was designed to accelerate low-energy electrons, achieving a maximum energy of approximately 94 MeV with a two-temperature energy spectrum ($T_1 = 7.0$ MeV and $T_2 = 16.0$ MeV) and a charge of 6.04 nC ($\mathcal{E} > 5$ MeV). The resulting electron bunch was then injected into the second stage, where hydrogen at a lower density ($n_a = 0.01n_{cr}$) was used, while the laser parameters were the same as in the first stage except that the waist was increased to $w = 8λ$. After the second stage, the electrons reached energies up to 225 MeV, with a two-temperature energy spectrum ($T_1 = 18.4$ MeV and $T_2 = 88.3$ MeV) and a charge of 4.55 nC ($\mathcal{E} > 5$ MeV). The self-injected electrons in the second stage reached a maximum energy of 123 MeV with a charge of 1.14 nC ($\mathcal{E} > 5$ MeV). The simulation results are compared with a theoretical DLA model, which describes the electron motion in the combined fields of the laser pulse and the quasistatic plasma channel. The model accounts for the transverse size of the channel by incorporating a Gaussian attenuation of the channel fields and off-axis injection. The theoretical model correctly describes the observed acceleration dynamics for both low-energy and pre-accelerated electrons, confirming its validity for designing multi-stage DLA schemes. Thus, the implementation of multi-stage acceleration by the DLA mechanism is successfully demonstrated for the first time in a numerical experiment.

title: Heat cleaning kinetics and thermal degradation of MOCVD-grown GaAs photocathodes
abstract: We evaluated metalorganic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD)-grown GaAs/GaAsP strained-superlattice photocathodes with integrated distributed Bragg reflectors in a low-voltage Mott polarimeter at Jefferson Lab. Without a protective arsenic cap, surface contamination can develop during transport and installation. Heat cleaning removes this contamination by thermally desorbing material bound to the surface, but excessive heating can also damage the photocathode. We modeled quantum efficiency (QE) in terms of surface contaminant coverage to describe its increase with heating time. QE rose more rapidly and reached a plateau nearly twice as high at $550^\circ\text{C}$ as at $450^\circ\text{C}$, while polarization remained near 83%. Further heating reduced QE and polarization. Reflectance measurements showed a shift of the optical resonance to shorter wavelengths, consistent with surface material loss. We also tested the cleaning method in a high-voltage photogun, where QE showed the same initial increase and subsequent decline. The cleaning procedure must therefore balance contaminant removal against loss of photocathode material.

title: The shear Alfvén continuum of optimized stellarators
abstract: The shear Alfvén continuum has been studied extensively in tokamaks, but its gap structure in modern optimized stellarators has received less attention, despite its importance for energetic-particle confinement in fusion pilot plants. We compute and compare the continua of five reactor-scale stellarator equilibria: two quasi-axisymmetric (QA), two quasi-helically symmetric (QH), and one quasi-isodynamic (QI). We present selective Fourier mode schemes that provide a sufficient resolution of eigenfrequencies within the frequency range of interest. In all five configurations, the widest gap is the HAE(2,$N_{\text{fp}}$) gap, which is driven by rotating ellipticity. This gap lies in the frequency range of strong resonance with prompt fusion-born alphas in the QA configurations but not in the QH and QI configurations, suggesting that QH and QI configurations may be easier to optimize for alpha confinement. Near-axis theory predicts the HAE(2,$N_{\text{fp}}$) and EAE gap widths well but overestimates the MAE gap widths and the gap widths of the QI configuration. These discrepancies likely arise from interactions between gaps, which depend on the rotational transform profile and are not captured by near-axis theory.

title: Single-Pulse Dosimetry for Ultra-High-Dose-Rate X-Ray Pulses Based on Radiation-Induced Acoustic Signals
abstract: Real-time dosimetry of ultra-high-dose-rate (UHDR) pulsed X-rays remains a major challenge. This proof-of-principle study investigates a dosimetry method for UHDR pulsed X-rays based on radiation-induced acoustic (RA) signals from a thin metal foil. The foil combines efficient X-ray absorption and acoustic resonance, converting deposited dose into acoustic signals with discrete resonant frequencies. Single-pulse measurements were performed at six dose levels spanning approximately 1--40 mGy(Si), with one pulse recorded at each level and instantaneous dose rates reaching the order of 10^6 Gy/s at the highest dose settings. The peak-to-peak amplified transducer-output voltage exhibited a linear relationship with the reference dose measured by thermoluminescent dosimeters (TLDs). These results demonstrate the feasibility of single-pulse acoustic dosimetry under the tested conditions. Furthermore, we establish analytical solutions for radiation-induced acoustic signals in a one-dimensional layered medium in both the time and frequency domains, providing a theoretical basis for signal interpretation and detector optimization.

title: Hot-Layer Ignition in High-Gain Inertial Confinement Fusion
abstract: Ignition of the shocked deuterium tritium shell is identified during the thermonuclear combustion of very high-gain targets in inertial confinement fusion (ICF). This mechanism is due to the local energy deposition of the fusion alphas created in this shocked shell, independently of hot-spot ignition, and generates sufficient energy to fully recompress the hot spot. A new analytical criterion for the ignition of the hot layer is presented. A simple three zone model, based on the thick layer hot-spot model, reproduces this mechanism, which breaks down into successive stages: ignition of the hot spot, compression of the shocked shell, ignition of the shocked shell, and subsequent recompression of the hot spot. 1D numerical simulations highlight the onset of this hot layer ignition thereby satisfying the analytical ignition criterion. It is shown that this mechanism amplifies the energy released by the combustion of the target by approximately 50 %.

title: Passivity Correction of the Thermistor Model in Bolometric Power Sensors and Its Dependence on Bead Temperature
abstract: This paper closes a series of works on thermistor bolometric power sensors, coaxial and waveguide, by treating what the two have in common. The per-state transformation m introduced in the waveguide work, which corrects the thermistor impedances of the model in each bridge state so that the two-port of the mount is passive, is analyzed on the eleven sensors of the preceding papers: the corrections are a few tenths of a percent in the coaxial mounts and one to two percent in the waveguide mounts, follow one pattern within each family, and the hottest state is the one whose efficiency departs most from the others. The transformation is tested by an independent measurement: the substituted powers of the three states, read with the manufacturer's procedure against a leveled source whose reflection is obtained from the closure of three Apollonius circles, give efficiency ratios of 0.999 +/- 0.016 and 0.997 +/- 0.008 (k = 2), which contain the values at the passivity floor (0.996, 0.998) and exclude those of the first pass (0.941, 1.023). Three sensors were swept in the bridge resistance, 23 and 31 states, and a fourth is treated apart: the correction reduces to one constant per state, the parallel resistance of the bead, represented by a law with one term scaling with the bridge resistance and one exponential in the bead temperature, with one thermal coefficient per family. The same property explains why the cross-ratio of four measured reflection coefficients, invariant under any state-independent two-port, departs from that of the four bridge resistances.

title: Chromatic calorimetry using nanocomposites: status and future challenges
abstract: The development of advanced detector technologies will play a key role in future high-energy physics experiments, such as the FCC-ee. In this context, chromatic calorimetry is an emerging concept for electromagnetic calorimeters, with the potential to combine the precise energy measurement of homogeneous calorimeters with longitudinal reconstruction of particle showers. The state of the art in chromatic calorimetry is reviewed, including experimental results from proof-of-concept prototypes and simulation studies investigating quantum-dot-based configurations. Recent progress and current challenges in the development of nanocomposites are also discussed. Finally, future prospects for chromatic calorimetry are outlined.

title: Continuous-Wave Operation at 30 MV/m of a Superconducting Radio-Frequency Gun Cryomodule with an Exchangeable Cathode Plug
abstract: A prototype 185.7 MHz superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) electron gun cryomodule has been developed for the proposed LCLS-II-HE Low Emittance Injector at SLAC. It has an in-situ ultra-high-vacuum exchangeable cathode plug system compatible with semiconductor photocathodes. With a copper plug, the gun achieved continuous-wave RF operation at a cathode field of 30 MV/m. No measurable degradation was observed after plug removal and reinsertion with the cavity at 4.4 K. This result is a significant improvement over past continuous-wave SRF gun systems with exchangeable plugs.

title: Edge transport mechanisms in small-ELM and type-I ELM regimes at JET using global gyrokinetic simulations
abstract: To explore tokamak operating regimes that combine high energy confinement with edge dynamics relevant for ITER, new regimes with small edge-localized modes (ELMs), referred to as baseline small-ELM (BSE), have been obtained at JET with the Be wall and W divertor. In this work, the edge transport mechanisms in a selected BSE discharge are compared with those in a standard H-mode with type-I ELMs using radially global gyrokinetic simulations with the GENE code. The simulations use experimental input profiles and include kinetic electrons and deuterium ions, electromagnetic (EM) effects, and the radially varying equilibrium $E\times B$ flow. At low toroidal mode number $n$, the type-I ELM pedestal is found to be unstable to kinetic-ballooning modes (KBMs), with radial mode structures covering the full pedestal. In the BSE regime, no KBM branch is found, and the same spectral range is dominated by hybrid ITG--TEM modes. The modifications of the linear modes by finite$-β$ effects are discussed in details. In nonlinear simulations of the type-I ELM regime, KBM-driven turbulence produces high transport levels that are resilient to the equilibrium $E\times B$ flow. By contrast, in the BSE regime, EM effects moderately increase transport, which is strongly regulated by the equilibrium $E\times B$ flow. The two regimes also differ in their radial turbulence organization and in the amplitude and persistence of the zonal shearing rate. These results identify the interplay between EM effects and equilibrium $E\times B$ flow as a key element of edge transport regulation.

title: nuSTORM: a unique GeV electron-(anti)neutrino machine
abstract: In this conference contribution, I briefly review current experimental programmes measuring the Dirac CP phase δCP using accelerator neutrinos. I argue that the nuSTORM concept---neutrino beams from a muon storage ring---could provide high-quality electron-(anti)neutrino beams needed for the cross-section inputs to δCP measurements.

title: Experimental Evidence for MeV Undulator Radiation Generated by Ultrarelativistic Positrons in a Periodically Bent Crystal
abstract: We report evidence for undulator radiation generated by ultrarelativistic positrons in a large-amplitude, long-period crystalline undulator. A pattern of Si$_3$N$_4$ stressors periodically bend the (110) planes of a Silicon crystal with a geometry measured independently by x-ray diffraction. Under planar alignment, the forward energy loss showed a localized excess at $6.8 \pm 0.3$~MeV ($4.05σ$), matching the predictions of simulations. Experimental results also indicate that an intense positron beam could make the undulator competitive in brilliance with state-of-the-art inverse-Compton gamma-ray sources.

title: Learning effective stochastic predator and prey dynamics across physical and biological systems from limited data
abstract: Constructing an effective low-dimensional stochastic model from sparse observations requires separating deterministic drift from state-dependent fluctuations when the governing interaction law is unknown. We formulate an adaptive neural stochastic differential equation with topology constraints (TC-AdaNSDE) for two-variable predator--prey dynamics. To regularize the inverse problem when data are scarce, the model combines flexible drift and correlated diffusion fields with density-adaptive local Kramers--Moyal moment estimates and soft phase-space constraints reflecting boundary saddle behavior near extinction and local stability near coexistence. Using a known nonlinear stochastic system, we first show that short-time trajectory error cannot assess diffusion accuracy on its own and must be paired with distributional measures of one-step transitions and long-time phase-space occupancy. We then apply this framework to macroscopic turbulence and zonal flow energies reduced from Hasegawa--Wakatani plasma simulations and to short ecological time series. In the sparse-data regime, TC-AdaNSDE reproduces both short-horizon evolution and long-time invariant energy distributions where deterministic reductions collapse and unconstrained stochastic fits diverge, while recovering physically interpretable drift and fluctuation fields across both physical and biological systems.

title: Optimizing MHz X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy with burst-mode free-electron laser operation
abstract: Burst-mode X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) provide a powerful platform for X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) experiments with sub-microsecond temporal resolution, but the achievable performance is constrained in practice by both photon statistics and the sample's dose tolerance. Here, we develop an analytical framework for estimating the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of pulsed XPCS measurements, including pulse-to-pulse fluctuations of the incident intensity. We combine this description with dose constraints and show that, for a fixed maximum dose, acquiring fewer frames at higher per-pulse intensity yields a higher SNR than distributing the dose over a larger number of low-intensity frames. The framework is validated against measurements at the European XFEL, where the intensity fluctuations of the investigated operation mode are found to cause only a negligible reduction in SNR. We further introduce and experimentally demonstrate a rolling bunch pattern with three pulses per train and variable pulse spacings. This scheme enables more than an order-of-magnitude increase in the accessible per-pulse intensity while maintaining equilibrium dynamics. Our results provide practical guidelines for optimizing dose-efficient MHz-XPCS experiments and for evaluating future XFEL operation modes.

title: 60-cm-long In-vacuum Zerodur Optical Cavity for Optical Lattice Atom Interferometry
abstract: Optical cavities are widely used in atomic physics experiments to control the spatial geometry and spectral properties of atom-light interactions. Recently, an optical lattice generated by the pristine mode of an optical cavity was utilized to hold and extend the quantum coherence of atomic spatial superpositions. Here, we describe an in-vacuum optical cavity designed to enhance the spatial and temporal coherence of optical lattice atom interferometers to one millimeter wavepacket separations and one minute measurement durations. The cavity uses a rigid Zerodur spacer to suppress the negative effects of thermal drift and mechanical-acoustic vibrations on the atomic motional state. The 60 cm-long cavity spacer provides ample optical access for the laser beams and imaging optics necessary for the preparation, quantum control, and read-out of the atomic state, as well as room for various source mass configurations for localized gravitational measurements. An integrated differential pumping structure enables compatibility with ultrahigh-vacuum operation and optical interferometry allows for in-situ vibration monitoring. The performance of the optical cavity is methodically characterized: we measure mirror vibration noise with amplitude below 5 nm/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$ in a wide frequency range of 2 Hz - 100 kHz and a slow 15 MHz thermal drift of the cavity resonance over 47 hours, which can be readily stabilized with an integrated piezo. The optical cavity supports both 852-nm light for Raman transitions and 1064-nm light for the optical lattice, with a free spectral range matched to an integer divisor of the cesium ground-state hyperfine splitting.

title: Experimental and Monte Carlo Simulation Studies to Characterize a Low-Pressure Gas-Based Positive-Ion Detector with a Nanometer-Equivalent Sensitive Volume
abstract: Compact low-pressure gas-based positive-ion detectors offer a promising approach to measuring particle track structure at the nanometer scale. These detectors use electric fields to collect and multiply positive ions produced by the incident radiation in mm-sized holes in dielectric materials, achieving a nm-equivalent spatial resolution of the localization of ionization events when scaled to liquid water at unit density.   In this work, a detector prototype featuring a 1.5 mm-diameter hole in a dielectric plate was experimentally characterized. Ion collection and multiplication were achieved by applying a negative high potential to the glass cathode 0.5~mm below the hole, assisted by a low drift field above the plate. A grounded readout electrode with a 0.8 mm hole covers the hole to prevent interactions of collected ions with the hole walls. The experimental setup was further modeled with Geant4-DNA and Garfield++ for deeper insight. By combining the measurements with the Monte Carlo simulations, a per-ion signal formation probability in the low single-digit percentage range was determined. Further, the signal formation mechanism, commonly attributed to ion-impact ionization within the hole, was critically examined. Ion-induced secondary electron emission from surfaces was considered a possible contributor to, or the primary mechanism of, signal formation that has not been addressed in detail in previous studies of this detector concept. Despite the extensive measurements and simulations, the available evidence did not reveal which physical processes governed signal formation or whether either mechanism dominates. We discuss key limitations in the current understanding of this detector class and propose future targeted measurements and simulations to clarify the signal formation mechanism and guide the development of compact positive-ion detectors and nanodosimeters.

title: Dephasing-free plasma acceleration with millijoule picosecond lasers
abstract: Laser-plasma accelerators reach gradients a thousand times above radio-frequency cavities, but need joule-class femtosecond lasers firing about once per second, and electrons outrun the wave. A comb of laser lines spaced by the plasma frequency, each in its own mode of a matched channel, drives a wake moving at the speed of light. In particle-in-cell simulations a 175\,mJ, 0.5\,ps drive holds 21\,GV/m over 10\,mm with a 0.15\,rad phase drift; a test electron gains 208\,MeV, 2.6 times more than in one mode. Because the wave builds up resonantly, the required energy falls steeply with density: a 29\,mJ drive sustains 20\,GV/m, and a 10\,mJ drive, within reach of kilohertz industrial lasers, gives a test electron 170\,MeV over 30\,mm. A simulated stage transfers 5\,\% of the laser energy to the wake; the Manley--Rowe limit is about 18\,\% for five lines.

title: Long-Term Stable Three-Axis Single-Beam Alignment-Based Atomic Magnetometer Using an Uncoated Buffer-Gas-Free Rubidium Ampoule for Unshielded Geomagnetic Monitoring
abstract: Optically pumped magnetometers achieve exceptional sensitivity, yet sustaining long-term baseline stability in unshielded Earth-field environments (~50,000 nT) remains challenging. We present the design, quantum-interference principles, calibration, and unshielded validation of a three-axis single-beam alignment-based atomic magnetometer built from an unmodified, uncoated, buffer-gas-free commercial rubidium (Rb) ampoule and a single 795 nm VCSEL. Pumped with $45^\circ$-oriented linearly polarized light on the $^{87}$Rb $D_1$ ($F=2 \to F'=1$) transition, the sensor exploits ground-state Zeeman quantum interference (rank-2 spin alignment), intrinsically cancelling first-order vector light shifts. Dual-zone 20 kHz AC heating ($75.0^\circ$C lower liquid Rb reservoir, $85.0^\circ$C upper optical zone) suppresses window condensation and thermal magnetic gradients over 29 days. Without buffer-gas pressure broadening, the VCSEL is stabilized via direct absorption spectroscopy at an optimized 3530 Hz dither frequency, eliminating odd-harmonic intermodulation leakage. A hybrid balanced polarimeter extracts $B_x$, $B_y$, and laser-lock errors from total absorption (sum channel) and $B_z$ from alignment-induced linear dichroism (difference channel) within an active zero-field compensation loop using a 12-bit microcontroller in a dual-stage mid-ranging architecture. Spectral analysis yields sub-LSB noise amplitudes of 0.5-5 pT at 1 Hz (15-150 $\mathrm{pT}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$), rolling off to 0.1-1 pT (3-30 $\mathrm{pT}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$) near 10 Hz. Continuous unshielded geomagnetic monitoring in Okayama benchmarked against synthesized Kakioka and Kanoya observatory records demonstrates high tracking fidelity and bounds instrumental bias instability to $\le 0.1$ nT at 100-200 s integration times.

title: Polarized positron generation via laser-engineered quasistatic magnetic fields in a spatially extended herringbone target
abstract: Polarized positron sources are of interest for precision studies of spin-dependent interactions and future high-energy colliders, yet their laser-driven realization remains challenging because of demanding laser or beam requirements. Here, we propose a target-engineered scheme for generating polarized positrons using a 3.4-PW single-color laser pulse and an initially unpolarized 10-GeV electron beam. Three-dimensional spin-resolved quantum electrodynamics particle-in-cell simulations show that laser-driven return currents in a herringbone target generate spatially extended quasistatic magnetic fields exceeding $\simeq 10^6$ T, with opposite polarities and a duration exceeding 100 fs. These fields correlate positron spin polarization with deflection direction, enabling angular selection of two oppositely polarized positron populations with polarization magnitudes of 63\% and a combined yield of approximately 0.007 positrons per incident electron, compared with a total yield of 0.029. Our results demonstrate a route toward highly polarized positron generation under laser conditions accessible to existing petawatt-class facilities, without requiring frequency-converted ultraintense fields or prepolarized incident beams.

title: Measuring and predicting plasma blob influence on downstream transport through paired simulations
abstract: We use two-dimensional TOKAM2D simulations of flux-driven turbulence to measure how much a single plasma blob affects particle transport farther out in the scrape-off layer. We evolve the same turbulent state twice, weakening the density and potential variations of one blob in one of the two simulations. The resulting difference in outward particle flux, integrated over time in each poloidal sector of a downstream band, defines the blob's influence vector $α$. Its magnitude falls steeply with distance from the band and generally increases with blob size and density content. Even blobs with similar bulk properties can differ in influence by orders of magnitude. A graph neural network that uses the recent evolution of the fields in and around each blob predicts much of this difference for pairs of otherwise similar blobs. To see how the difference develops, we compare the downstream density and radial velocity in the two simulations. For both strongly and weakly influential blobs in the pairs examined, changes in radial velocity account for most of the local change in outward flux. In the stronger responses, the density and flow contributions tend to reinforce each other in the same sectors at the same times.

title: A conservative latent neural ODE for stiff collisional-radiative plasma kinetics
abstract: Collisional-radiative (CR) models govern the non equilibrium population kinetics of partially ionized plasmas and are a dominant cost in integrated edge and divertor plasma simulations, where a stiff system of dozens to thousands of coupled rate equations must be solved at every spatial cell and time step. We present a two-stage machine learning (ML) surrogate that replaces the direct CR solve with a compact, continuous-time, deployable dynamical model. Stage~1 is a grey-box autoencoder that compresses a high-dimensional ion population vector into a low-dimensional latent space in which four coordinates, one per charge state of the lithium system studied here, are \emph{fixed} to the physical charge-state distribution and the rest are learned. Stage~2 is a latent neural ODE that learns the continuous-time evolution of the latent variables. We (i) integrate in a density-folded, logarithmic clock on which the latent trajectory is smooth enough for an explicit integrator, (ii) sample time adaptively by latent arc length so the sharp ionization transition is resolved, (iii) add a linear damping toward an estimate of the CR steady state as a design choice, and (iv) enforce mass conservation directly. The surrogate is accurate, with a charge-state error that is unchanged under refinement of its output grid, over full-trajectory rollouts within the trained horizon, and exactly conservative: on $1480$ held-out trajectories at the trained conditions it reproduces the charge-state evolution with a median absolute error of $4.2\times10^{-3}$ on fractions in $[0,1]$, conserves mass to $10^{-7}$, {and evaluates a full sixteen-decade trajectory in ${\sim}76\,μ$s per trajectory in batched inference on a single GPU.} A model retrained with whole $(\nA,\Te)$ grid points withheld is equally accurate at those unseen conditions.

title: Ultrashort pulsed laser atmospheric filament properties and microwave radiation inferred from S-band guided wave interaction and self-emission
abstract: The electrical conductivity $σ$ of the plasma filament left behind by an ultrashort pulsed laser (USPL) optical pulse after it is geometrically then self-focused in air via the Kerr effect is measured by attenuation of a $3.2$ GHz TE$_{10}$ mode within an S-band waveguide through which the filament passes, taking into account the characteristic radius $R$ of the filament, as determined by fast camera visible light imaging. Models of the major air constituents' ionization rate $W_{i}$ vs. local laser intensity $I$, and of electron temperature $T$ and mean axial electron momentum $\left\langle p_{z}\right\rangle $ vs. peak laser intensity $I_{0}$ are then used to infer the filament's $I_{0}$, $T$, major species particle densities, current decay rate $ν$, and current time integral $Q$ after pulse passage. $Q$ is independently measured via the filament's self-emission in the waveguide signal for comparison. The theoretical far field microwave radiation pattern for the later $Q=Q\left( z\right) $ is calculated. It compares favorably to published measurements, provided $ν$ is reduced to the value where the total radiated power is equal to the center-of-mass electron kinetic energy imparted by the laser's magnetic Lorentz force. Results are presented for a $30$ cm long filament at a broad range of atmospheric pressures.

title: Coherence Lengths of Laser Pointers
abstract: We report on the coherence lengths of low-cost green laser pointers in the midst of multimodal behavior using an optical interferometer based on noncollinear beam geometries and a CMOS detector array. Examined devices include three diode lasers and a frequency-doubled neodymium-emission diode-pumped solid state (DPSS) laser. Coherence length measurements are variable among devices, but values can nevertheless regularly exceed 10 cm. The work serves as a template for an advanced undergraduate physics laboratory experiment and may inspire new kinds of laser pointer devices utilizing interference effects as operative principles.

title: Impact of Environmental Stress on Low Gain Avalanche Diode Sensors Response
abstract: Low Gain Avalanche Diodes or LGADs are silicon sensors capable of achieving excellent timing resolution due to their characteristic internal gain. Detectors based on LGAD technology play a crucial role in High Energy and Nuclear Physics experiments, among other applications. However, their performance is affected by environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, and storage conditions. A systematic evaluation of the response of LGAD sensors as a function of these environmental parameters is therefore of essential importance for any application. LGAD sensors fabricated at the Brookhaven National Laboratory are characterized and stress-tested against various operating conditions, such as rapid temperature and humidity changes. Dedicated and detailed simulations are used to interpret the experimental results.

title: The Simons Observatory: A Novel Design for Heat Strap at Sub-Kelvin Temperatures
abstract: We present a novel process for the fabrication of copper heat straps and a measurement of their thermal performance at sub-Kelvin temperatures. The conductance of the heat straps is consistent with the bulk conductivity of annealed copper over the range 60 mK to 1 K. We find no evidence for deviation from a linear dependence of conductivity with temperature over the explored range, indicating that the contact resistance at the strap ends is sub-dominant. Heat straps developed and validated through the described process have been deployed in both the Large Aperture Telescope Receiver and a Small Aperture Telescope of the Simons Observatory and have met thermal requirements.

title: Nonlinearly Causal General-Relativistic Superfluid Hydrodynamics: Simulating Vortex Dynamics in Neutron-Star Interiors
abstract: Neutron stars provide a natural laboratory for superfluid matter under extreme conditions. Its nonlinear dynamics is central to pulsar glitches, their possible links to fast radio bursts, and tidal interactions in inspiralling binaries. We develop a general-relativistic superfluid hydrodynamics framework incorporating entrainment, vortex forces, and line energy, and derive, for the first time, necessary and sufficient conditions for nonlinear causality and strong hyperbolicity. We also show that commonly used dissipative, force-balanced formulations without line tension are generically ill-posed at short wavelengths because of the Donnelly-Glaberson instability.   Exploiting the analogy between vortex arrays with tension and force-free electrodynamics, we recast vortex dynamics in terms of effective electric and magnetic fields and drift velocities. This motivates a new finite-volume scheme combining constrained transport of superfluid vorticity with implicit electric-field evolution, enabling stable numerical evolution of the full system. We validate the scheme using an exact solution to the relativistic superfluid Riemann problem and Kelvin-wave dispersion relations, among other tests.   Finally, we simulate dynamical, global general-relativistic two-fluid neutron-star equilibria, validate their oscillation modes, and present the first simplified calculation of superfluid interior spin-down with prescribed vortex release and repinning. The resulting stationary state retains both a net twist in the vortex array and residual differential rotation of the superfluid. Our framework thus enables nonlinear numerical studies of general-relativistic superfluid dynamics in neutron-star interiors.

title: Hydrodynamic modeling of liquid metal field emitter deformation under combined RF and DC magnetic fields
abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) breakdowns, also known as vacuum (or electrical) arcs and breakdowns, or electrical discharges, have been studied for over decades, but the mechanisms of the RF breakdown are still questionable. This phenomenon reduces the stability of the beam, damages the RF cavities, and thus limits the achievable accelerating field in the particle accelerator. In the case of Muon Collider, the RF cavities have to withstand an electric field of the order of multi tens of MV/m and a DC magnetic field of a few tens of teslas, with a minimum rate of RF breakdown. Different models have been proposed, and some important factors that could lead to the RF breakdown have been identified, such as the field emission current, irregularity of the surface , presence of hot particles on the surface and the role of the DC magnetic field. In this paper, we give insights to the mechanism of RF breakdowns using a hydrodynamic and a magnetohydrodynamic approach, focusing on understanding the forces that deform the liquid copper emitter. We found that if the local RF electric field is sufficiently high, it could provoke the emission of hot copper droplets into the cavity. Our simulations use the computational fluid dynamics module, the magnetic and electric field module, and the level set method in the COMSOL software to simulate the behavior of a copper liquid emitter with the Navier-Stokes equation under the influence of the pressure radiation, and the surface tension force.

title: Future avenues for precision oscillation measurements with compact movable reactors
abstract: No planned neutrino experiment is expected to surpass Daya Bay's precision on $\thone$. Doing so requires innovative strategies to reduce statistical and systematic uncertainties. In this study, we consider a futuristic program with a movable reactor antineutrino source placed within short distances ($L\lesssim 3\,\km$) from the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) detector. Due to the large fiducial mass of JUNO, even a relatively small reactor can produce a statistically significant number of events over a few years to probe the $\lesssim 8.7\% \,\nuebar$ disappearance set by $\thone$. We consider two possibilities: a $\mathcal{O}(20\mwth)$ microreactor in alcoves of the access tunnel to the underground laboratory, and a $\mathcal{O}(400 \mwth)$ unit on the surface. In both cases the reactor is observed by a small flux monitor detector near the source, while JUNO measures the antineutrino flux at two baselines, suppressing correlated flux and detector systematics. Using the measured Daya Bay per-isotope spectra and its covariance, we model a high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) core for the microreactor and a low-enriched uranium (LEU) core for the surface unit, and discuss various potential sources of systematic uncertainties and their impact on the precision of $\thone$. The underground microreactor could improve on JUNO's reach by a factor of three to four, to $\relsth \simeq 4\%$ over a decade, while the surface reactor would reach the present global-fit precision, $\relsth=2.5\%$, in about three years, provided the emission rate is monitored across reactor relocations to the sub-percent level.

title: Aggregating soft-photon recoil with a positive finite-step sampler
abstract: We model stochastic radiation reaction by aggregating soft photons into one positive recoil, retaining the local no-emission probability and two loss moments of the crossed-field QED kernel. Unlike Gaussian diffusion, the sampler preserves one-sided energy loss. Analytical synchrotron moments expose a finite-step cooling bias, which state feedback reduces. Laser and ion-channel tests probe excessive-loss risk and directed radiation spectra, providing a practical route to stochastic particle simulations without resolving individual soft emissions.

title: High-Power Short-Wavelength Frequency Comb from Coherent Radiation of Uncompressed Electron Beams
abstract: High-power frequency combs at short wavelengths would open new opportunities for precision measurements and high-resolution spectroscopy. Here, we propose a frequency comb based on coherent undulator radiation from uncompressed electron bunches. An optical frequency comb serves as the seed, establishing a common phase reference for microbunching in successive electron bunches and transferring its phase coherence to short-wavelength harmonic radiation. By exploiting interference between distinct laser-induced microbunching pathways, we reduce the sensitivity of the harmonic bunching phase to electron-beam energy fluctuations, a major challenge for maintaining interpulse coherence. Start-to-end simulations demonstrate frequency comb generation in the vacuum-ultraviolet (148 nm) and soft X-ray regimes, yielding average radiation powers of approximately 1 W and 100 mW, respectively, with approximately 6 $μ$W and 100 nW concentrated in individual comb teeth. These results establish a promising route toward high-power, phase-coherent short-wavelength frequency combs for precision spectroscopy, including searches for the nuclear transition in trapped $^{229}$Th ions.

title: Quantum Zeno Effect with a Superposed Measurement Schedule in Relational Time
abstract: Motivated by the Page-Wootters construction in which time is a quantum clock reading and the global system state is stationary, we propose a quantum circuit that explores the observable consequences of treating measurement timing as a quantum degree of freedom. We place two Zeno measurement schedules of a driven qubit in a coherent superposition using a schedule qubit. We show that, for a fixed drive strength, the interference visibility between the two schedules depends only on the time offset between them, not on the number of intermediate measurements taken. Then we show that, for one schedule-readout outcome, the Zeno trend reverses, predicting a result that complements the standard Zeno probability. We propose a circuit implementation with physical memory qubits and show that measuring the memory register's joint $X$-basis parity distinguishes a coherent schedule from a classical or dephased one. We give the gate count and an error budget for a superconducting-qubit implementation. The Page-Wootters picture motivates this protocol and provides an equivalent stationary representation, although the predictions follow from the standard circuit description without requiring a relational-time interpretation. This is consistent with the Page-Wootters framework recovering standard quantum dynamics through correlations between a clock and the rest of the system.

title: Compact GridPix Tracking: Test Beam Performance and Detector Response Modelling
abstract: We characterise a Timepix-based GridPix detector with a 21 mm drift length using 2.6 GeV electrons at ELSA. Tracks entering through the window at several angles are reconstructed as compact $μ$TPC tracklets, providing position and local direction from one layer. Measured angular widths are approximately 5--10 mrad. An empirical response model calibrated to these data augments Geant4 ionisation information with gas-transport and readout effects, reproducing ten of twelve angular widths within approximately 20% and all spatial-residual widths within approximately 12%. Application without re-tuning to an independent 5 mm-drift measurement shows larger angular discrepancies. Our response model therefore provides input to feasibility studies of future compact tracking detectors.

title: Resonant filling for long-pulse operation of EuXFEL using iterative learning based feed forward
abstract: A future operation scenario of the European XFEL (EuXFEL) is long-pulse (LP) mode, where the 800 superconducting radio frequency (SRF) cavities of the linac are energized with RF pulse lengths of up to 500ms. Compared to the current, short-pulse (SP) mode with less than 2ms, the dominant mechanical eigenmodes of the cavities at a few hundred Hertz pose a significant control challenge, as the RF pulse extends beyond a multiple of their periods. To improve energy efficiency of LP operation, cavities are operated at bandwidths in the range of tens of Hertz, a factor of 10 narrower than in SP. Due to peak power limitation of the proposed high power amplifiers, even the fill time surpasses mechanical mode periods. This paper presents experimental evaluation of two feed forward adaptation approaches to facilitate resonant-filling despite mechanical mode transients: In a single-cavity regulation setup, the RF drive phase is adjusted to match the Lorentz force detuning induced cavity phase shift. In vector-sum RF regulation systems, the incident phase cannot be adjusted to each cavity individually, so the concept is inverted by adapting mechanical cavity tuner drives to match each individual cavity resonance trajectory with a fixed common RF drive phase.

title: A Paired Monte Carlo Intensity-Ratio Method for Incorporating Detector Resolution in Amplitude Analysis
abstract: Finite detector resolution can bias resonance parameters and fit fractions extracted from amplitude analyses. We present the paired Monte Carlo intensity-ratio method for incorporating resolution effects into amplitude analysis. The method uses ratios of reference intensities evaluated at paired truth-level and reconstructed kinematics to reweight the Monte Carlo normalization and approximately account for detector resolution. A resampling study of simulated $D^+\to K^+π^+π^-π^0$ decays shows that the method substantially reduces resolution-induced shifts in fitted resonance widths. Likelihood evaluation uses intensity calculations and normalization sums, avoiding a response convolution at each data event.

title: SlotFlow-GB: A Neural Framework for Trans-Dimensional Inference of Overlapping Galactic Binaries
abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will observe the millihertz gravitational-wave sky, including millions of long-lived Galactic binaries (GBs), tens of thousands of which are expected to be individually resolvable throughout the mission's lifetime. Extracting these sources requires jointly determining their number and physical parameters from strongly overlapping signals, posing a computationally demanding trans-dimensional inference problem. We introduce SlotFlow-GB, a neural framework that constructs a learned approximation to the trans-dimensional posterior, producing a probability distribution over source multiplicity and parameter densities for individual binaries in a single evaluation, without requiring their number to be specified in advance. We demonstrate this framework using year-long LISA simulations containing up to ten binaries within a 2 $μ$Hz frequency interval, focusing on a high-SNR regime in which source overlap, rather than individual-source detectability, is the primary challenge. The inferred source count differs from the true count by at most one in 94% of cases, while the model identifies individual binaries even when their signals overlap strongly in frequency. A complete evaluation, including parameter sampling, takes just 41 ms per band on one NVIDIA GH200 GPU, or 530 ms on eight laptop CPU threads. We further demonstrate that these distributions can be used to initialize subsequent likelihood-based inference, connecting fast amortized predictions with joint parameter estimation.

title: momipy: A time-resolved momentum microscopy data analysis workflow
abstract: Photoemission momentum microscopy is an emerging approach to photoelectron spectroscopy that is transforming electronic band structure mapping at both laboratory-based and large-scale facilities. Its extension to time-resolved measurements has recently enabled major advances, ranging from the femtosecond imaging of exciton wavefunctions to dark-field photoelectron microscopy of light-induced dynamics and strong light-matter interactions. However, the rapid acquisition of high-dimensional data sets (including electron in-plane momenta $k_x$ and $k_y$, kinetic energy $E_\mathrm{kin}$, time $Δt$, and more) poses substantial challenges for data handling and analysis. A typical workflow encompasses data acquisition, exploratory visualization, calibration and targeted feature extraction, with data management ideally guided by FAIR principles. Here, we present momipy, a Python package that streamlines the momentum microscopy data analysis workflow efficiently and at low computational cost. Among other features, momipy provides interactive 4D data visualization, energy and momentum calibration, space-charge correction, and a broad selection of multidimensional data analysis routines, including binning, momentum-map extraction and time-, energy- and momentum-resolved model fitting. momipy is accompanied by a selection of interactive example scripts, supporting adoption of momipy by both experienced researchers and users new to momentum microscopy.

title: Energy transfers in decaying three-dimensional Hall-magnetohydrodynamics turbulence: Dependence on the Ion-Inertial Length and the Magnetic Prandtl Number
abstract: We present a systematic study of energy transfers in three-dimensional (3D) decaying Hall-magnetohydrodynamics (HMHD) turbulence. Our study has been designed to investigate the dependence of these transfers on initial energy spectra, the ion-inertial length $d_{i}$, and the magnetic Prandtl number $Pr_{m}$. Using shell-to-shell decomposition, we compute the energy transfer rates for (a) kinetic-to-kinetic, (b) magnetic-to-magnetic, (c) kinetic-to-magnetic, and (d) magnetic-to-kinetic interactions by carrying out extensive pseudospectral direct numerical simulations (DNSs) of 3D HMHD and its MHD counterpart. Furthermore, we examine the magnetic-to-magnetic and current-density-to-magnetic energy transfers arising from the Hall term in this framework. Energy transfers between like fields -- namely, kinetic-to-kinetic and magnetic-to-magnetic -- are predominantly local and forward in direction, cascading energy from large to small length scales. This behavior is consistent with a self-similar flow structure in the inertial range. Cross-field transfers, between kinetic and magnetic energy, are found to be forward but non-local in character. At low and high $Pr_{m}$, the transfers become local, and the nonlinear energy transfer is significantly suppressed. Moreover, we observe that the Hall term drives both inverse and forward transfers of magnetic energy, associated with local and non-local transfer, respectively.

title: How zonal states beat-driven by Alfven eigenmodes stabilize micro-turbulence in tokamak plasmas
abstract: The effects of zonal states (ZS) beat-driven by Alfven eigenmodes (AEs) on micro-turbulence stability are investigated; taking toroidal Alfven eigenmode (TAE) and ion temperature gradient mode (ITG) as an example. The analysis is carried out by deriving the nonlinear gyrokinetic equation describing particle response to ITG, in the presence of TAE beat-driven ZS. It is found that, the phase space zonal structure generated by AEs could lead to a significant reduction in the local nonuniformity drive and, thereby, stabilize the local ITG instabilities. The zonal flow induced shearing, on the other hand, contributes only to a real frequency shift and, typically, negligibly small additional stabilization.

title: Direct measurement of the on-shot focal-spot size of a kilojoule-class petawatt laser
abstract: We report a direct, on-shot determination of the focal-spot size of a kilojoule-class, four-beam petawatt laser. Encircled-energy curves were inferred from the energy transmitted around aluminum-coated spheres of varying diameters placed at the focal plane. The 50% encircled-energy diameter D50 of each beam was obtained by fitting a two-component Gaussian mixture with Bayesian inference. With all deformable mirrors optimized in closed loop, the best-corrected alignment beam reached D50 = 34 (+4/-5) um, three times the diffraction limit of 10 um. Under full-power conditions, the thermal distortion of the main amplifier broadened this beam to D50 = 102 (+9/-8) um and reduced its peak intensity ninefold, to 2.2 (+0.6/-0.9) x 10^18 W/cm^2 at 250 J and 1.3 ps. The energy fraction of the narrow component decreased from 68% to 38%. These reference values serve facility users, and a deformable mirror upstream of the pulse compressor, now on one beam only, doubles the on-shot peak intensity.

title: Design of an electrostatic violin mode damper for gravitational wave detector enhancement
abstract: The test mass suspension fiber resonances and their harmonics pollute the sensitivity of the detectors of the advanced Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (aLIGO) and cause operational issues. The current method of damping these violin modes requires the GW detector be locked; identifying modes after a test mass replacement takes valuable commissioning time, and modes which are close together in frequency are hard to distinguish and damp independently. We present the design, prototyping, and initial lab testing of an electrostatic violin mode damper: a compact sensor and actuator set next to the fiber to monitor and damp resonances. The design uses a split photodiode and LED integrated into a shadow sensor, and an electrostatic actuator. The device is vacuum compatible and its mechanical design is compatible with the suspension and surrounding cage of the advanced Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory test masses. The shadow sensor has a shot noise limited displacement noise floor of 5e-11 {\meter\per\sqrt\hertz}, sufficient to measure the test mass violin modes when highly excited. The modeled actuator strength is 0.3 nN, meeting the requirements to damp the modes for the aLIGO suspensions.

title: Superheating field of clean superconductors near the type-I--type-II boundary: the low-temperature Meissner stability limit of niobium
abstract: We calculate the low-temperature superheating field $B_{\rm sh}$ of clean superconductors near the boundary between type-I and type-II superconductivity, with particular emphasis on Nb. Ginzburg--Landau theory is not applicable at low temperatures, while previous microscopic calculations have been limited to either the large-$κ$ regime or the dirty limit. The clean, low-$κ$ regime relevant to Nb has therefore remained unresolved. We solve the self-consistent nonlinear nonlocal Eilenberger problem for the Meissner state and then analyze its stability against small perturbations. For a Nb-like material with $κ_{\rm GL}=0.7$, we obtain $B_{\rm sh}\simeq 290\,{\rm mT}$ at $T/T_c=0.2$, using $B_{c0}\simeq 200\,{\rm mT}$. For a TESLA-shaped Nb accelerator cavity, this corresponds to an intrinsic Meissner-stability limit of about $67\,{\rm MV/m}$.

title: A new efficient and accurate approximation for the dielectric function of the weakly coupled electron gas
abstract: An accurate analytic approximation is developed for the real boundary component of a regularised, causal complex auxiliary function describing the random phase approximation dielectric response of the weakly coupled electron gas across classical to strongly degenerate conditions. Its collisionless imaginary boundary component is known exactly from the Fermi--Dirac occupation logarithm. Following an assessment of existing approximations and the establishment of a high-precision numerical benchmark, a two-regime representation is constructed: a $6/7$ rational function at weak and moderate degeneracy and a composite polynomial approximation at strong degeneracy. Exact asymptotic constraints determine the rational denominator algebraically, leaving six independent state functions. Branch-locked optimisation, Chebyshev parametrisation and Bernstein-basis constraints provide accurate, smooth and numerically pole-free behaviour. In the strongly degenerate regime, the logarithmic Kohn contribution is isolated explicitly, with its regular remainder represented by analytically integrable polynomial expansions. The approximation achieves a maximum relative error of approximately $0.11\%$ in the real dielectric integral across the investigated domain, accurately reproduces its scaled derivative and is substantially faster than numerical quadrature. Validation using the electron--electron dynamic structure factor and imaginary-time correlation function yields maximum plasmon peak-amplitude errors of approximately $1.04\%$ and maximum pointwise correlation-function errors below $0.166\%$. Comparisons with established approximations demonstrate substantial improvements, particularly for weakly damped collective excitations. The resulting model provides an accurate, computationally efficient foundation for electronic screening, dynamic dielectric calculations and X-ray Thomson scattering analysis.

title: The role of externally-driven density fluctuations in the enhancement of beam spray
abstract: Speckled laser beams, commonly used to ionize and heat plasma for inertial confinement fusion and high-energy-density experiments, are shown to drive long-wavelength plasma-density fluctuations that induce beam spray in other laser beams. Experiments show that a 1053 nm beam undergoes increased beam spray when 351 nm speckled heater beams are on. These observations indicate that the high-intensity speckles sustain an increased level of steady-state density fluctuations. Modeling of these fluctuations predicts amplitudes that are orders of magnitude larger than the level of thermal fluctuations. Beam propagation simulations show increased beam spray due to self-focusing and filamentation when heater-driven density fluctuations are included.

title: Electron Scattering with ASTRA: Helium and Molecular Hydrogen
abstract: We present an implementation of electron-impact scattering in \ASTRA{}~(AttoSecond TRAnsitions)~[J. M. Randazzo {\it et al.}, Phys. Rev. Research {\bf 5}, 043115 (2023)], a general close-coupling method for the molecular electronic continuum based on transition density matrices and already employed for molecular photoionization. The scattering states are obtained with a pole-free Galerkin method with variational surface matching, which yields the scattering matrix and, from it, the elastic and electronically inelastic integral cross sections and the molecular-frame differential cross sections. For helium, \ASTRA{} reproduces elastic and inelastic cross sections over a broad energy range, resolves the $\mathrm{He}^{-}(1s2s^2\,{}^2S^e)$ Feshbach resonance in both energy and angle, and reproduces the interference features in the angular distributions for $1s^2\to1s 2\ell$ excitations observed experimentally. For molecular hydrogen, the elastic and inelastic cross sections closely reproduce the benchmark results obtained with \UKRmolplus{} for the same close-coupling expansion. We also report orientation-resolved, three-dimensional molecular-frame angular distributions for state-resolved electron-impact excitation, which are shown to depend strongly on the molecular orientation. These results validate the method in view of its application to larger molecular targets.

title: 4D-TEMPO: Differentiable 4D-STEM ptychography via fast Physics Optimizers
abstract: Electron ptychography recovers atomic structure from 4D-STEM data: diffraction patterns at multiple positions of a scanned probe. Current codes reconstruct an image and read atoms off it, or fit atoms under an $L_1$ loss; neither gives per-atom uncertainty. We propose 4D-TEMPO, a differentiable physical renderer that fits the atoms, the microscope, and the detector directly to the recorded electron counts under a Poisson likelihood. The output is a list of atoms, each a Gaussian primitive with a 3D position, a thermal width, and a model-conditional error bar from the Fisher information. The Fisher information also conditions the solver, gives the dose (electrons per Å$^2$) each parameter needs, and separates calibration from imaging. On a simulated WSe$_2$ bilayer, starting from the published reconstruction, fitted atoms cut in-plane error by a third (3.2 vs. 4.8 pm) and depth error by 40-61% against its 3D peaks. Depth comes from multiple scattering into the dark field, the faint counts outside the direct beam. The two layers, $10\times$ closer than the depth of field, separate; per-atom depth then follows the layer geometry. When the model is well specified, the bars are calibrated (69% of position coordinates within $1σ$). On experimental WSe$_2$, fitted atoms predict held-out patterns better than the three published codes we test. With free probe modes where atoms are incomplete, the same likelihood predicts best on all three held-out benchmarks, matches every WSe$_2$ baseline in 5 min against up to 20.5 h, and passes torchslice at its released setting 180$\times$ sooner on PrScO$_3$. Per-atom error bars, planned doses, and fast reconstruction point to low-dose, real-time 3D imaging of beam-sensitive and dynamic materials.

title: Depth-enhanced molecular imaging with two-photon oblique plane microscopy
abstract: High-numerical-aperture (NA) oblique plane microscopy enables noninvasive fluorescence imaging of subcellular dynamics without radical sample modification. However, performance degrades at depth in multicellular specimens as scattering and refractive-index heterogeneity raise out-of-focus background. We report a two-photon oblique plane microscope that improves resolution at depth by combining high-NA single-objective detection with multiphoton plane illumination. The microscope achieves $\sim\!300$ nm lateral and $\sim\!650$ nm axial resolution, with single-molecule sensitivity and $<\!60$ nm localization precision in vivo. Compared with two-photon point scanning, the lower illumination NA delivers order-of-magnitude lower peak intensity, enabling $>\!5\times$ faster volumetric acquisition (up to $3.25 \times 10^6$ voxels s$^{-1}$). In multicellular contexts, near-infrared nonlinear excitation enhances contrast throughout the illumination depth by $\sim\!2\times$ and restores volumetric resolving power by $>\!2\times$ relative to linear excitation. We demonstrate these capabilities through molecular imaging of epithelial tissue, stem-cell-derived gastruloids, and living fruit fly embryos, including multicolor transcription-factor dynamics, optogenetic subcellular control, and single-mRNA tracking, all using standard glass-based mounting.

title: Optical readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors with SiPMs
abstract: Scintillation light readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors (MPGDs) is used for imaging and track reconstruction applications including in optical Time Projection Chambers (TPC). Typically, high resolution CCD or CMOS imaging sensors are used and PMTs can be employed to obtain auxiliary timing information. We report on the optical readout of MPGDs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) which enables limited spatial resolution. Arrays of SiPMs were used to read out Gaseous Electron Multipliers (GEMs) and Glass Micromegas amplification stages. Center of gravity reconstruction of hit positions yields a spatial resolution of approximately 1.35 mm for signals shared across multiple SiPMs. High gain of the amplification stage as well as the SiPMs enables good signal sharing and is advantageous for position reconstruction.

title: Numerical study of nitrogen oxides chemistry during plasma assisted combustion in a sequential combustor
abstract: Plasma Assisted Combustion (PAC) is a promising technology to enhance the combustion of lean mixtures prone to instabilities and flame blow-off. Although many PAC experiments demonstrated combustion enhancement, several studies report an increase in NOx emissions. The aim of this study is to determine the kinetic pathways leading to NOx formation in the second stage of a sequential combustor assisted by Nanosecond Repetitively Pulsed Discharges (NRPDs). For this purpose, Large Eddy Simulation (LES) associated with an accurate description of the combustion/NOx chemistry and a phenomenological model of the plasma kinetics is used. Detailed kinetics 0-Dimensional reactors complement the study. First, the LES setup is validated by comparison with experiments. Then, the NOx chemistry is analyzed. For the conditions of operation studied, it is shown that the production of atomic nitrogen in the plasma by direct electron impact on nitrogen molecules increases the formation of NO. Then, the NO molecules are transported through the turbulent flame without being strongly affected. This study illustrates the need to limit the diatomic nitrogen dissociation process in order to mitigate harmful emissions. More generally, the very good agreement with experimental measurements demonstrates the capability of LES combined with accurate models to predict the NRPD effects on both turbulent combustion and NOx emissions.

title: Fundamental-derivative criticality of ion-acoustic solitons in fluid-Poisson plasmas with general equations of state
abstract: Non-ideal ion compressibility modifies the nonlinearity of ion-acoustic waves. In a fluid-Poisson plasma with Boltzmann electrons and a barotropic ion equation of state, we relate the quadratic KdV coefficient to the fundamental derivative of the effective acoustic pressure. Its vanishing marks loss of genuine nonlinearity. Higher derivatives of the equation of state determine whether the cubic reduction is focusing or defocusing and govern the quartic-flux reduction at simultaneous criticality. The exact Sagdeev formulation resolves compressive and rarefactive soliton branches and their Gardner unfolding. Exact continuation identifies an equation-of-state-controlled rarefactive double-layer boundary distinct from both the cubic critical point and an orbitwise pressure-slope threshold. As they approach this boundary, solitons develop a logarithmically widening flat top, and the exact Sagdeev quadrature quantitatively captures the standard saddle-passage law. Along the boundary toward the acoustic codimension-two point, exponential localisation lengths diverge while the amplitude vanishes. Full fluid-Poisson simulations confirm finite-time propagation of selected exact stationary profiles. Our results connect acoustic criticality, exact orbit admissibility, and equation-of-state-controlled solitary waves in dispersive plasmas.

title: FPGA-based LQG controller and hardware-in-the-loop simulator implementation for nanomechanical systems
abstract: We present an open-source framework for real-time Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation on the affordable Red Pitaya STEMlab FPGA platform. The controller implements a discrete-time Kalman filter and Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) for systems with up to three coupled oscillatory degrees of freedom, targeting applications in levitated optomechanics, MEMS/NEMS, and related experimental platforms. Complementing the controller, the HIL simulator provides a~configurable second-order stochastic plant with nonlinear input and output mappings, enabling realistic closed-loop testing under real-time and fixed-point constraints. A MATLAB-based workflow automates model configuration, controller synthesis, numerical scaling, and FPGA deployment without requiring specialized hardware expertise. As an end-to-end demonstration, we present the stabilization of a levitated nanoparticle in a two-dimensional double-well potential, illustrating the complete workflow from model definition and simulation to real-time feedback control.   The codebase: https://github.com/TU-Wien-ACIN-CDS/FPGA-based-LQG-and-HIL-simulator-for-nanomechanical-systems

title: The Numerics of VMEC++
abstract: VMEC++ is a Python-friendly, from-scratch reimplementation in C++ of the Variational Moments Equilibrium Code (VMEC), a fixed- and free-boundary ideal-MHD equilibrium solver for stellarators and tokamaks. The first VMEC implementation was written by Steven P. Hirshman and colleagues in the 1980s and 1990s and its latest Fortran incarnation (PARVMEC, https://github.com/ORNL-Fusion/PARVMEC) is widely used in stellarator optimization systems. Our work improves on previous implementations with regard to various critical aspects: special care has been put in providing an idiomatic Python experience, from installation to actual usage; VMEC++ has a zero-crash policy; it supports inputs in the classic INDATA format as well as friendlier JSON files. VMEC++ execution times are typically less than or equal to previous implementations, and time to convergence can be decreased dramatically by leveraging its hot-restart feature: by providing the output of a VMEC++ run as initial state for a subsequent one, VMEC++ is initialized using the previously converged equilibrium. This can dramatically decrease runtimes when running on many similar magnetic configurations as it typically happens in stellarator optimization pipelines. On the flip side, some features of the original Fortran VMEC implementation are not yet available in VMEC++, such as support for non-stellarator-symmetric configurations. This contribution presents the internal numerics of the open-source VMEC++ package publicly for the first time.
